title: Overview and justification
body:
Three things shape how you get on at university: how you learn, how you are assessed, and the feedback you get along the way. Some students meet these one at a time and treat them as separate hurdles. This course proposes a different view. It shows how learning, assessment and feedback work together as one cycle, one you will meet again and again throughout your studies. Understanding how these parts of academic studies connect is worth your attention right at the start, because it lets you study with purpose from the outset rather than spend your first terms working it out the hard way.

Over five short lessons you will look at what learning at university actually asks of you, and at how university spells out what you are meant to learn. You will then look at what assessment is really for, at how to make feedback worth having, and finally at how the three connect into a single cycle you can run deliberately. None of it is abstract: it all applies to the work you are already doing, this term, in whatever you are studying. By the end you will have a clearer picture of how your own studies work, and a few practical habits for making each piece of work feed the next.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course you will be able to:

_items.text: apply an understanding of how university learning works to your own study
interpret your own assessment tasks and marking criteria
act on feedback to improve your own work
align your own academic practice with the learning, assessment and feedback cycle.

title: In real academic practice
body:
Everything in this course applies to the work you are already doing. Every module you take sets assessments, marks them against criteria, and gives you feedback; the students who understand that cycle, and run it on purpose, are the ones whose work improves from one assignment to the next rather than repeating the same mistakes. Treat what follows as being about your own essays, reports and exams, not about study in the abstract.

The same brief, standard, feedback and next-task cycle runs in many areas of professional practice. You are given a brief, your work is judged against a standard, you receive feedback, and you carry it into the next task. Learning from that feedback and iterating your practice on the back of it is a habit you keep long after you graduate.

title: Signpost
body: Learning, assessment and feedback are not three separate things. They form a cycle: what you learn is tested by assessment, assessment produces feedback, and feedback, once you act on it, feeds your next round of learning. Select each part of the cycle to see what the course covers. In the final lesson you will see how the three connect into one cycle you can run on purpose.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle to find out what the course covers.

_items.title: Learning
_items.body: Learning at university is not the same as at school: more of it is in your hands, and the point is to understand and use ideas, not just collect them. The first two lessons look at what that shift asks of you, and at how each module spells out what you are meant to learn.

_items.title: Assessment
_items.body: Assessment is how your learning is tested, through essays, exams, presentations and more. It is not there to catch you out: it shows you, and your tutors, how your learning is going. The third lesson looks at what assessment is really for, and at how to read what a task is asking of you.

_items.title: Feedback
_items.body: Feedback is what you get back on your work, and it is the part students most often waste. Used well, it is your tutors telling you what to do differently next time. The fourth lesson looks at the forms feedback arrives in, and at how to work out the action a comment is really asking for.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: University asks you to learn in a way that may feel new. At school, learning often meant taking in what you were told and giving it back accurately. Here, you are joining a community of people who make, test and argue about knowledge, and learning means taking part in that work. This lesson looks at what that shift involves, and why it shapes everything else you will do at university.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are at the start of your time at university, and the way learning works here may be new to you. At this stage you are not expected to know it all already; you are expected to begin finding your feet. This lesson looks at what learning at university asks of you, so that the habits you build now set you up well for the years ahead.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify what makes learning at university different from learning at school
recognise the discourse community of your own subject
distinguish surface learning from deep learning in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A discourse community is a group of people who share a way of making and testing knowledge: how they ask questions, what counts as good evidence, and how they reach agreement. Every subject at university is its own discourse community, with its own habits of argument.

Learning here is less about collecting facts and more about joining that community. You learn how your subject thinks, not only what it has concluded. This matters because it changes what getting better means: progress is not storing more information, but taking a fuller part in how your subject builds knowledge.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Where do you sit in your subject's discourse community right now, and what would moving toward its centre look like for you?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Learning at university means joining your subject's discourse community: a group that makes, tests and argues about knowledge together. You can now identify what makes that different from school, and begin to recognise the community of your own subject. The move from surface to deep learning, and the habits that support it, will matter in every lesson that follows.

title: Orientation
body: Every module you take is built around a short list of learning outcomes: statements of what you should be able to do by the end of it. They are easy to skim past, but they are the clearest signal your tutors give of what your learning is for. This lesson looks at where to find them and how to read one closely, because once you can, you can see exactly what your assessment will ask of you.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: Early in your degree, the way a university organises its teaching can feel unfamiliar: modules, learning outcomes, and timetables that leave much of the work in your hands. This is normal, and it is something you grow used to. This lesson shows you how that structure fits together, so you can see what is expected of you and plan your own time with more confidence.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify the learning outcomes in one of your own modules
break a learning outcome into its active verb and what it asks you to demonstrate
describe how teaching in {{context}} is organised to build your learning.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A learning outcome is a statement of what you should be able to do by the end of a module. It describes what you will be able to demonstrate, not just what will be covered in class. Every module is built around a set of these, usually printed in the module handbook or on its page in your virtual learning environment.

They matter because your assessment is, in effect, asking you to evidence and demonstrate them. The outcome tells you what you are aiming at; the assessment is where you show you have reached it. Learning to read an outcome closely is one of the most useful habits you can build early, because it tells you what success actually looks like.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Find the learning outcomes for one of your own modules. Pick one that you are not sure how to show you have met. What do you think it is actually asking you to do?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Learning outcomes are the statements of what each module expects you to be able to do, and they are where your assessment points. You can now find the outcomes in your own module's documentation, and break one down into its active verb and what it asks you to demonstrate. Reading outcomes this way turns a vague aim into a clear target, and it is a habit that will help in every module you take.

title: Orientation
body: Assessment is one of the words students worry about most, and often one of the least explained. At university it takes many forms, and it is almost always tied to what your learning outcomes asked you to do. This lesson looks at the range of ways you are assessed, and at one distinction that changes how you should treat a task: whether it is formative or summative.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: In your first year, assessment at university can look very different from what you met at school or college. It comes in more forms, and more of it is left in your hands. You are not meant to have mastered all of it yet. This lesson sets out the forms assessment takes and what each is for, so you can approach every task knowing why it has been set.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise the range of ways you are assessed at university
tell formative and summative assessment apart in your own modules
explain the purpose an assessment in psychology serves.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Assessment is how your work is judged against the standards of your subject. At university it can be broad in approach and takes many forms. In one way or another it is almost always present, because it is how your tutors see whether you have met a module's learning outcomes.

Reading an assessment well, knowing what kind of task it is and what it is for, lets you give it the right kind of effort rather than guessing. That starts with seeing how varied assessment is, and with one distinction that changes how much a task counts.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look at the assessments for one of your own modules this term. Which are formative and which are summative, and does knowing the difference change how you would approach them?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Assessment at university is far wider than exams: essays, presentations, portfolios, reflective pieces, practice-based tasks and exams are all ways your work is judged against your subject’s standards. You can now tell formative assessment, which helps you improve and does not count, from summative assessment, which sets your grade. More than that, you can see how they work together: formative tasks are where you find out what is not yet working and put it right, so that by the time a summative task counts you are already performing at your best. This is what strategic learning means: recognising why each task has been set and what it is preparing you to do, because every formative and summative task is a step towards the same thing, being able to demonstrate your module’s learning outcomes. Once you can see that link, you can tell what any task is really asking of you and put your effort where it counts, in every module you take.

title: Orientation
body: Feedback is one of the most useful things university gives you, and one of the easiest to waste. It is almost never just a mark: it is your tutors telling you what to do differently next time. This lesson looks at the forms feedback arrives in, and at the skill that makes it worth having - working out the action a comment is actually asking you to take.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: Early on, feedback at university can be easy to misread: brief, unfamiliar in its wording, and not always the praise you might hope for. That does not mean you are doing badly. This lesson helps you see what feedback is for and how to act on it, so that from the start you treat it as something that moves your work forward rather than something to set aside.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise feedback in the different forms it arrives in
identify what a piece of your own feedback is telling you
turn one piece of feedback in {{context}} into a specific next action.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Feedback is comments on and insights into your work, given to help you improve. It is much more than a grade: it arrives in many forms - a mark, written comments on your script, annotations in the margin, spoken feedback in a tutorial, a completed marking rubric, even comments from peers.

Whatever form it takes, feedback is only useful once you work out what it is asking you to do next. That last step, reading the action behind the words, is the skill this lesson builds.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of feedback you have had, at school or university. What was it actually asking you to do differently, and did you do it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Feedback is the comments and insights that tell you how to improve, and it arrives in many forms, not just a mark. You can now recognise those forms, and, the skill that makes feedback worth having, work out the action a comment is really asking you to take. Reading the action behind the words, and acting on it, is what turns feedback into better work next time.

title: Orientation
body: This lesson pulls the earlier ones together. You have looked at what learning at university asks of you, at what assessment is for, and at how to use feedback. Here you will see how those three connect: not as three separate things to deal with one at a time, but as one cycle, where each part feeds the next. Seeing the cycle is what lets you work with it rather than against it.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: As you settle into your first year, it helps to see how the parts of studying connect rather than meeting each one alone. Learning, assessment and feedback are not separate events; they are one cycle you move through again and again. This lesson draws them together, so you can see the pattern early and make it work for you across every module.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: show how learning, assessment and feedback connect rather than stand alone
recognise the learning, assessment and feedback cycle in your own experience
plan one change to how you study {{context}} using the learning, assessment and feedback cycle.

title: Concept: definition
body:
It is easy to treat learning, assessment and feedback as three separate things: you learn in lectures and reading, you are assessed in essays and exams, and feedback turns up afterwards. Dealt with one at a time, each can feel like a hurdle to clear and then forget.

They work far better understood as one connected cycle, where each part feeds the next and the whole thing comes round again. Understanding that connection is what this lesson builds, because it is the difference between repeating the same cycle and improving with each turn of it. In a moment you will map out how the parts follow on from one another; first, it is worth seeing why thinking of them as a loop changes how you study.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think back over one module you have taken. Can you see the cycle in it, where your learning led to assessment, assessment to feedback, and feedback (if you used it) back to learning? Where did the cycle break for you, and why?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Learning, assessment and feedback are easiest to deal with one at a time, but they work as one connected cycle, where each part feeds the next and the whole comes round again. You can now show how they connect rather than stand alone, and recognise that cycle in your own experience of a module. Seeing the loop is what lets you carry effort from one part into the others, so that each piece of work becomes the start of the next improvement rather than a repeat of the last.

title: Put the cycle in order
body: These four stages make up the learning, assessment and feedback cycle, but they only work in one order, each depending on the one before. Can you put them in sequence, from first to last?
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). You can try as many times as you like.
ariaQuestion: Put the four stages of the learning, assessment and feedback cycle in order from first to last.

_items.text: You learn something new, in lectures, reading and seminars.
You are assessed on it, through an essay, exam, presentation or another task.
You receive feedback on how you did.
You act on that feedback, which feeds your next round of learning.

_feedback.correct: That's the cycle. Learning leads into assessment, assessment produces feedback, and feedback, once you act on it, feeds your next round of learning. They form one connected loop rather than four separate steps, which is why feedback is worth having and assessment is worth preparing for.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. Think about what has to happen before each stage can: you cannot be assessed on what you have not learned, and feedback comes after the assessment, not before it. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some of those are in the right place, but not all. Each stage depends on the one before it, so work out what has to come first and try again.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students finish a module with the same comment on their final essay: a solid summary, but you needed to take more of a position of your own.

{{learner-a}} treats learning, assessment and feedback as three things that happen and then end. The module is over and the mark is in, so the comment is read once and filed away. Nothing about it changes how {{learner-a}} approaches the next module, and when the next essay comes back the same comment is there again: the cycle has simply repeated.

{{learner-b}} treats the same comment as the start of the next round rather than the end of this one. It becomes something to act on: {{learner-b}} plans the next essay around taking a clear position, and carries that into how the new material is read and revised from the outset. The next piece of work takes a position, and it is stronger, because the feedback fed back into the learning.

Both got the same comment. Only {{learner-b}} treated the three as one cycle, letting feedback feed the next round of learning. That is what connects them, and it is what turns each piece of work into the start of the next improvement rather than a repeat of the last mistake.

title: Working with the cycle
body: Use these to keep the cycle turning in your own studies, rather than treating each module as a fresh start.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: When a module begins, have I looked back at feedback from a related one?
Am I clear what each assessment is actually asking me to show?
When feedback arrives, have I read all of it, not just the mark?
Have I turned that feedback into one or two things to carry into my next piece of work?
Do I treat each piece of work as the start of the next round, rather than the end of this one?

title: Formative check: how the three connect
displayTitle: Why is it more useful to think of learning, assessment and feedback as one cycle rather than three separate stages?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to think of learning, assessment and feedback as one cycle?

_items.text: Because each one feeds the next: learning is what assessment draws on, assessment produces feedback, and feedback changes how you learn next time.
_items.feedback: Yes. Treated as a cycle, each part feeds the next, so the work you do in one place pays off in another.

_items.text: Because it means you only have to do one of the three, not all of them.
_items.feedback: No. The cycle is not a shortcut; it is about how the three connect, not about leaving any out.

_items.text: Because assessment matters and the other two do not.
_items.feedback: No. The point of the cycle is that all three matter and depend on each other, not that one replaces the others.

_items.text: Because it lets you skip feedback once your marks are good enough.
_items.feedback: No. Feedback is the part that feeds your next round of learning, so it is worth having whatever your marks.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Seen as a cycle, learning, assessment and feedback each feed the next, so effort in one place carries through to the others. That is why none of them is worth treating as a one-off.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the three have to do with each other, rather than whether you can do fewer of them.
_incorrect.final: The three form a cycle because each feeds the next: learning is what assessment draws on, assessment produces feedback, and feedback changes how you learn next time. It is about how they connect, not about leaving any out.

title: Formative check: the cycle in your experience
displayTitle: A student does well in one essay, reads the feedback, and uses it to plan the next essay, which comes back stronger. Which part of the learning, assessment and feedback cycle did using that feedback feed back into?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which part of the cycle did using the feedback feed back into?

_items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay improved.
_items.feedback: Yes. Acting on feedback feeds the next round of learning, and that is what the cycle is for.

_items.text: Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
_items.feedback: No. Feedback comes at the end of one round, but acting on it is exactly what starts the next.

_items.text: Only the mark on the first essay, which cannot now change.
_items.feedback: No. The mark on the first essay is fixed, but the feedback still shapes what comes next.

_items.text: The deadline for the next essay.
_items.feedback: No. A deadline is part of the task, not part of the learning the feedback feeds.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Using feedback to plan the next piece of work feeds it straight back into your learning, closing the loop and starting the next round stronger. That is the cycle working as it should.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student did with the feedback, and what improved as a result.
_incorrect.final: Acting on feedback feeds your next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay was stronger. The mark on the first essay cannot change, but the feedback still shapes what comes next.

title: Assessment introduction
body:
This is the test for the whole course. It covers everything you've studied in the lessons, with a set of questions to work through.

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.
A student says: "I just need to memorise everything the lecturer says and repeat it back in the assessment." Why is this a weak approach to university learning?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student says: "I just need to memorise everything the lecturer says and repeat it in the exam." Why is this a weak approach to university learning?

_items.text: Because university learning is about understanding and using ideas, not just reproducing them; most assessments reward what you can do with the material.
_items.feedback: Yes. University rewards what you can do with ideas, not how much you can repeat.

_items.text: Because lecturers do not say anything worth memorising.
_items.feedback: No. Lectures are worth attending; the point is to understand, not only memorise.

_items.text: Because memorising anything is impossible at university.
_items.feedback: No. Memory still matters; it just is not the whole of learning here.

_items.text: Because assessment never draws on what is covered in lectures.
_items.feedback: No. Exams often do draw on lectures, but they ask you to use the material, not just recall it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. University learning is about understanding and using ideas, which is what most assessment rewards.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what university assessment actually asks you to do with what you learn. Try again.

body: You are starting a new module and want to know what you will actually be expected to be able to do by the end. Where should you look first?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You are starting a new module and want to know what you will actually be expected to be able to do by the end. Where should you look first?

_items.text: The module's learning outcomes.
_items.feedback: Yes. Learning outcomes state what you should be able to do by the end.

_items.text: The total length of the reading list.
_items.feedback: No. The reading supports the module, but it does not state what you must be able to do.

_items.text: The number of lectures each week.
_items.feedback: No. The timetable tells you when you meet, not what you must be able to do.

_items.text: The name of the lecturer.
_items.feedback: No. Who teaches it does not tell you what you are expected to achieve.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A module's learning outcomes tell you what you should be able to do by the end.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which part of a module states what you must be able to do. Try again.

body: An essay brief says: "Critically evaluate the two main approaches." What is it mainly asking you to do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: An essay brief says: "Critically evaluate the two main approaches." What is it mainly asking you to do?

_items.text: Weigh the two approaches against each other and judge their strengths and weaknesses, rather than just describing them.
_items.feedback: Yes. "Critically evaluate" asks for judgement, not just description.

_items.text: List everything you know about both approaches.
_items.feedback: No. Listing is description; the brief asks you to evaluate.

_items.text: Choose whichever approach is easier to write about.
_items.feedback: No. You need to weigh both, not avoid the harder one.

_items.text: Summarise the lecture that introduced the topic.
_items.feedback: No. A summary is not an evaluation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. "Critically evaluate" asks you to weigh and judge the approaches, not just describe them.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at the instruction word and ask what kind of thinking it calls for. Try again.

body: Why is it worth reading a task's marking criteria before you start writing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it worth reading a task's marking criteria before you start writing?

_items.text: Because the criteria tell you what the marker is actually looking for, so you can aim your work at it.
_items.feedback: Yes. The criteria are what your work is judged against, so they tell you what to aim for.

_items.text: Because the criteria replace the need to do any reading.
_items.feedback: No. Criteria guide your work; they do not replace the reading.

_items.text: Because the criteria tell you the submission deadline.
_items.feedback: No. The deadline is in the brief; the criteria are about quality, not timing.

_items.text: Because the criteria are identical for every task, so reading them once is enough.
_items.feedback: No. Criteria vary by task, so they are worth reading each time.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The marking criteria tell you what the marker is looking for, so you can aim your work at it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the criteria are for when your work is marked. Try again.

body: A tutor writes on your essay: "You describe the theory but do not evaluate it." What action is this feedback asking you to take next time?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A tutor writes on your essay: "You describe the theory but do not evaluate it." What action is this feedback asking you to take next time?

_items.text: Go beyond describing the theory to weighing it up and judging how convincing it is.
_items.feedback: Yes. The comment asks for evaluation, not more description.

_items.text: Add more description so the account is thorough.
_items.feedback: No. The comment asks for less description and more evaluation.

_items.text: Remove the theory from the essay altogether.
_items.feedback: No. The theory belongs there; it needs evaluating, not cutting.

_items.text: Simply make the essay longer.
_items.feedback: No. Length is not the issue; the kind of thinking is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The comment asks you to evaluate the theory, not just describe it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Work out what the comment wants you to do differently, not just what it says. Try again.

body: You get the same comment, "your structure jumps around", on two essays in a row. What does this most likely mean you should do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You get the same comment, "your structure jumps around", on two essays in a row. What does this most likely mean you should do?

_items.text: Treat it as a recurring issue, and research how to structure your argument so you can address it before you write the next one.
_items.feedback: Yes. A repeated comment is a pattern to act on: find out how to structure your argument better, and apply it next time.

_items.text: Ignore it, since a comment only matters once it appears three times.
_items.feedback: No. A comment that recurs is already worth acting on.

_items.text: Change your subject so the comment stops coming back.
_items.feedback: No. The issue is structure, not the subject.

_items.text: Wait for the tutor to fix the structure for you.
_items.feedback: No. Acting on feedback is your part of the cycle, not the tutor's.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A comment that comes back is a recurring issue: research how to structure your argument, and address it in your next piece.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a repeated comment is telling you to change. Try again.

body: Put the four stages of the learning, assessment and feedback cycle in order, from first to last.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop).
ariaQuestion: Put the four stages of the learning, assessment and feedback cycle in order, from first to last.

_items.text: You learn new material.
You are assessed on it.
You receive feedback on how you did.
You act on the feedback, which feeds your next round of learning.

_feedback.correct: That's the cycle. Learning leads into assessment, assessment produces feedback, and acting on feedback feeds your next round of learning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. You cannot be assessed on what you have not learned, and feedback comes after the assessment. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some are in the right place, but not all. Each stage depends on the one before it, so work out what has to come first. Try again.

body: Why is feedback worth paying attention to even after you already have the mark for a piece of work?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is feedback worth paying attention to even after you already have the mark for a piece of work?

_items.text: Because acting on it feeds your next round of learning, so it improves the work that comes after, not the mark you already have.
_items.feedback: Yes. Feedback is for the next piece of work, which is what makes the cycle worth running.

_items.text: Because acting on it can change the mark you have already been given.
_items.feedback: No. The mark is fixed; the value of the feedback is in what comes next.

_items.text: Because feedback only ever applies to the single piece of work it is written on.
_items.feedback: No. Its real value is in carrying across to your next piece of work.

_items.text: Because ignoring feedback breaks the university's rules.
_items.feedback: No. It is not a rule; it is that using feedback is how your work improves.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Acting on feedback feeds your next round of learning, which is the point of the cycle.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what feedback can change, given the mark is already set. Try again.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Now that you have finished the course, rate each statement again. You will then see how your confidence has changed.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_patterns.rose: Your confidence in {{item}} has grown over the course.
_patterns.stayedHigh: You were confident about {{item}} and remain so.
_patterns.stayedLow: {{item}} still feels uncertain. It would be worth revisiting this before you move on.
_patterns.noMovement: Your confidence in {{item}} has not shifted much.
_patterns.dropped: Your confidence in {{item}} has fallen. This often reflects a more accurate view of what is involved rather than a step backwards, and noticing it is itself progress. It would be worth another look.

_summary._predominantlyUp: Your confidence grew across most of these.
_summary._mixed: Your confidence grew in some areas and settled lower in others. Both are useful to know.
_summary._flatOrLow: Several of these still feel unsettled, which is worth knowing now.

_feedback._standalone: Here is where your confidence sits on each statement.

_forward._summative: The check ahead is where this confidence will be tested.
_forward._application: The real measure will be how this holds up when you next apply it in your own work.

title: Course summary
body:
You have reached the end of the course. You now have more than a set of facts about university study: you have a way of working strategically. You can take a deliberate, strategic approach to developing your own learning and academic practice throughout your studies, rather than meeting each module, assessment and piece of feedback as it comes. In particular, you can:

  • apply an understanding of how university learning works to your own study: you have seen what learning at university asks of you, and how modules set out what you are meant to learn;
  • interpret your own assessment tasks and marking criteria: you can read what a task is really asking of you;
  • act on feedback to improve your own work: you can work out the action behind a comment and carry it into your next piece;
  • align your own academic practice with the learning, assessment and feedback cycle: you have seen how the three connect, and how to run them as one cycle rather than three separate steps.

You have just rated your confidence again on the previous page. Comparing it with the check you took at the start is your own measure of how far you have come.

title: In real academic practice
body:
You now have a way of seeing your own studies that will serve you in every module from here on. Each assessment you meet is a chance to show what you have learned, each piece of feedback a pointer to what to do next, and the two together are how your work improves across the degree. The habit to keep is simple: read what each task is asking, use the feedback you get, and let it shape the next piece of work.

That same habit carries into professional life. Wherever you are given work, judged against a standard, and told how to improve, the people who get better are the ones who treat each round as feeding the next. The cycle you have just learned to see is one you will use long after you graduate.

title: Where this goes next
body:
This is an introductory course: it gives you the shape of how learning, assessment and feedback work together. You can take it further from here.

Go deeper on this topic. The Intermediate and Advanced tiers of Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback take the same cycle further, into harder cases and more of your own judgement.

Put it into practice. Other pathways in this programme apply what you have just learned. Academic Writing is where most of your assessed work is produced and most feedback lands. Criticality develops the kind of thinking that higher-level assessment rewards. Reflective Practice turns on a similar iterative cycle, where you act, reflect on how it went, and carry what you learn into your next attempt, so the habit you have built here transfers straight across.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four steps in how you join your subject’s community. Turn each card, in order, to see how you move from the edge towards the centre.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all four.

back.body: The people who make, teach and debate knowledge in your subject: researchers, tutors and students. Each subject is its own discourse community, and learning here means finding your place within it. Because knowledge is built between people rather than alone, taking part in that shared work is itself how you learn.

Knowledge is not static, it develops and accepted understanding evolves. Academic communities propose, test and make new knowledge. A discourse community does this by the questions it asks, what it accepts as good evidence, and how it argues towards agreement. To learn your subject is to learn not only its current understanding of the field but also its debate, discussion and discourse.

Knowledge is not a fixed set of facts to memorise it is not static. Rather it is the interpretations the community itself debates and refines through the process of discourse. Currently accepted understanding is the knowledge that emerges from ongoing debate, and so it can be added to, it can and does change.

At first you work with ideas your community has already agreed or is still debating. As you progress, you begin to apply, support and contest those ideas and practices yourself, moving from the edge of your subject towards its centre, and with practice, becoming a contributor to its discourse through your own interpretations and the knowledge you generate.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students preparing for the same seminar on the same reading.

{{learner-a}} reads the chapter once and highlights the key terms, ready to repeat the definitions if asked. The reading has been covered and the facts are in place. This is surface learning: the information has been taken in, but it sits on its own.

{{learner-b}} reads the same chapter and keeps asking why. Why does the author reach this conclusion? How does it fit with last week's idea? Where might someone in the field disagree? By the seminar, {{learner-b}} can connect the reading to a wider debate and take a position within it. This is deep learning: the ideas are linked into understanding that can be used and argued.

Both students have done the reading. Only {{learner-b}} has taken the step your discourse community values, turning information into understanding.

title: Sense-making habits
body: These habits move you from surface learning toward taking a fuller part in your subject. Use them as you study this week.
instruction: Tick each item once you have done it.

_items.text: Have I asked why an idea matters, not only what it says?
Have I looked for how this week's ideas connect to last week's?
Have I put the main idea into my own words?
Have I noticed where experts in my subject disagree, and tried to see why?
Have I asked a question in a seminar, or written one down to raise?
Have I read one thing beyond the set reading this week?

title: Formative check: university versus school learning
displayTitle: Which of these best describes how learning at university differs from learning at school?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option best describes how learning at university differs from learning at school?

_items.text: You mainly take in and give back what you are told.
_items.feedback: This is closer to how learning often works at school. At university you are expected to do more than receive and return information.

_items.text: You take part in making and testing knowledge, not just receiving it.
_items.feedback: Yes. This is the shift that defines university learning.

_items.text: You rely on your tutor's notes as the only source you need.
_items.feedback: Your tutor's notes are a starting point, not the whole of your subject's knowledge.

_items.text: University is the same as school, only with harder material.
_items.feedback: It is not only that the material is harder; what you are asked to do with it changes.

_feedback.correct: That's right. University learning means taking part in how your subject makes and tests knowledge, rather than simply receiving it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you are asked to do with knowledge at university, not just how much of it there is.
_incorrect.final: The key difference is that university learning means taking part in making and testing knowledge, not just receiving it. Taking in more, relying only on the tutor's notes, or treating it as simply harder each miss that shift.

title: Formative check: recognising your discourse community
displayTitle: Which of these would best help you recognise the discourse community of your own subject?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option would best help you recognise the discourse community of your own subject?

_items.text: Noticing who produces and debates the key work in the field, and how they argue.
_items.feedback: Yes. The community shows itself in who makes the knowledge and how they argue about it.

_items.text: Counting how many facts your textbook contains.
_items.feedback: A count of facts tells you little about how your subject makes or tests knowledge.

_items.text: Learning the timetable for your lectures.
_items.feedback: Useful to know, but it tells you nothing about how your subject thinks.

_items.text: Memorising the names of your tutors.
_items.feedback: Knowing names is not the same as seeing how the community debates and agrees.

_feedback.correct: That's right. You recognise a discourse community by seeing who makes its knowledge and how they argue, not by counting facts or learning logistics.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about how knowledge is made and argued, rather than facts or logistics.
_incorrect.final: You recognise your subject's discourse community by noticing who produces and debates its key work, and how they argue. The other options are about quantity or logistics, not how the community makes knowledge.

title: Inside a learning outcome
body: A learning outcome is short, but it has parts. Open each one to see what it is doing.
instruction: Select each part to open it. Work through all of them.

_items.title: The active verb
_items.body: Every outcome turns on a verb: analyse, evaluate, describe, apply. The verb tells you the kind of thinking you must show, and it is usually the first thing to find.

_items.title: What it is about
_items.body: After the verb comes the subject of the outcome: the material, skill or situation the verb acts on. This tells you where to point your effort.

_items.title: How you demonstrate it
_items.body: An outcome is only met when you show it. Ask what would count as evidence: a judgement reached, a method applied, a case explained. This is what your assessment will look for.

_items.title: Why it matters
_items.body: Read this way, an outcome stops being a vague aim and becomes a target you can work toward. If you know the verb, the subject and what counts as evidence, you know what your work has to do.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students read the same learning outcome from their module handbook: Evaluate the usefulness of a common method in your field.

{{learner-a}} reads it quickly and starts describing the method: what it is, how it works, where it is used. The writing is accurate, but it only describes. The outcome asked for something the writing never does.

{{learner-b}} reads the same outcome and breaks it down first. The verb is evaluate, which means weighing strengths against weaknesses to reach a judgement. What it is about is the method's usefulness, not simply how it works. And demonstrating it means coming to a reasoned view, backed by evidence, about when the method helps and when it does not. {{learner-b}} then writes to exactly that.

Both students know the method. Only {{learner-b}} answered the outcome, because only {{learner-b}} worked out what it was actually asking.

title: Breaking an outcome down
body: Use these on any learning outcome, before you start the work it leads to.
instruction: Tick each item once you have done it.

_items.text: Have I found the active verb in the outcome?
Do I know what that verb is actually asking me to do?
Have I identified what the outcome is about, the subject the verb acts on?
Have I worked out what would count as evidence that I have met it?
Have I checked which assessment task this outcome is tied to?

title: Formative check: recognising a learning outcome
displayTitle: Which of these is a learning outcome, rather than another part of a module handbook?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is a learning outcome rather than another part of a module handbook?

_items.text: By the end of this module, you will be able to evaluate competing explanations of a problem.
_items.feedback: Yes. It states what you will be able to do, built around a verb to aim at.

_items.text: This module runs for twelve weeks, with a two-hour lecture each Monday.
_items.feedback: This is the module's schedule, not a statement of what you will be able to do.

_items.text: The module is worth twenty credits at Level 4.
_items.feedback: This is an administrative detail, not an outcome you demonstrate.

_items.text: Reading: three set chapters and one journal article each week.
_items.feedback: This is the reading list, not a learning outcome.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A learning outcome states what you will be able to do, built around a verb you can aim at. The others are schedule, credits and reading: useful, but not outcomes.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that says what you will be able to DO by the end, not how the module is run.
_incorrect.final: A learning outcome states what you will be able to do by the end, built around a verb (here, 'evaluate'). The schedule, the credit value and the reading list are all parts of a handbook, but none of them is an outcome you demonstrate.

title: Formative check: reading the verb in your own outcome
displayTitle: You are breaking down a learning outcome from your own subject that begins with the verb 'analyse'. Which of these shows you have understood what that verb asks for?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option shows you have understood what the verb 'analyse' asks for?

_items.text: Separating something into its parts, examining how they relate, and saying what that shows.
_items.feedback: Yes. 'Analyse' asks you to break something down and show what the parts reveal.

_items.text: Listing everything you can remember about the topic.
_items.feedback: Listing is recall, not analysis. The verb asks for more than coverage.

_items.text: Giving your personal opinion of the topic.
_items.feedback: An opinion on its own is not analysis; analysis works from the parts and the evidence.

_items.text: Describing the topic clearly from start to finish.
_items.feedback: Describing tells what something is; analysing shows how its parts work and what they mean.

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'Analyse' asks you to break something into its parts, examine how they relate, and show what that reveals, not to list, describe or simply give an opinion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what 'analyse' does that listing, describing or giving an opinion does not.
_incorrect.final: 'Analyse' asks you to separate something into its parts, examine how they relate, and draw out what that shows. Listing is recall, describing is just an account, and an opinion alone has no working behind it.

title: The forms assessment takes
body: Assessment comes in many forms. Turn each card to see what it is, what it asks of you, and the skills that help you do it well.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all six.

back.body: A written argument in response to a question or title. You take a position and support it with evidence and reasoning, in your subject’s style. To do well you need to build a clear line of argument, select and weigh evidence, and structure your writing so a reader can follow the reasoning. The essay is common because it makes your thinking visible: a marker follows how you reach a conclusion, not only the conclusion itself. That is why a strong essay reads as one connected argument rather than a set of separate points.

You explain or argue something aloud, often with slides, to tutors or peers. It assesses how clearly you can communicate ideas, not only hold them. Succeeding draws on organising material for a listener, speaking clearly to time, and using visuals that support rather than crowd what you say. It is set because so much academic and professional work depends on being understood by others, not only on being right. The clearer you make a complex idea for your audience, the more you show you have understood it yourself.

A collection of work gathered over time, sometimes with a reflective commentary. It shows how you have developed, not just a single finished piece. It rewards steady organisation, honest self-review, and the ability to show progress by selecting and explaining the right pieces. A portfolio is used when how you got there matters as much as the final result, so it rewards work built steadily rather than assembled at the last minute. Choosing what to include, and saying why, is itself part of what is assessed.

Writing in which you examine your own learning: what you did, what you noticed, and what you would change. The thinking is the point. Doing it well means looking honestly at your own practice, connecting experience to ideas from your subject, and drawing out what you will do differently. It is assessed because learning from experience is a skill in its own right, one you will use throughout your studies and your working life. What earns credit is honest, specific insight into your own practice, not a tidy account that avoids any difficulty.

A timed assessment under set conditions. It tests what you can recall and do without your notes to hand. Success rests on secure recall, planning an answer quickly under time pressure, and applying what you know to the question actually asked. Exams test what you can do independently, with no support to hand, which is why they reward secure understanding over last-minute memorising. Practising under timed conditions beforehand is what turns what you know into what you can show on the day.

An assessment of what you can do in practice: a laboratory or studio task, a clinical or professional placement, a performance, or fieldwork. It judges applied skill and professional judgement in a real or realistic setting, not only what you can write about it. To do well you need to apply knowledge to the task in front of you, work safely and to your field’s standards, and show sound judgement as conditions change.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students are given the same draft essay to hand in for comments. It is a formative task: the tutor will mark up the draft, but the grade will not count. The graded essay comes later.

{{learner-a}} sees that the draft does not count and puts little into it, handing in a rough attempt and barely reading the comments that come back. When the graded essay is due, {{learner-a}} makes the same mistakes the comments had already flagged.

{{learner-b}} treats the draft as a chance to find out what is not working yet. The comments point out a weak line of argument, so {{learner-b}} reworks it before the graded essay. The final piece is stronger, because the formative task did its job.

Both students did the same formative task. Only {{learner-b}} used what it is for: formative assessment is there to help you improve before the summative assessment that sets your grade.

title: Approaching an assessment
body: Use these when a new assessment appears on a module, before you start it.
instruction: Tick each item when you have checked it.

_items.text: Have I found out what form this assessment takes?
Do I know whether it is formative or summative?
If it is summative, do I know how much it is worth?
If it is formative, have I planned to act on the feedback before the task it prepares me for?
Have I checked which learning outcomes this assessment is testing?

title: Formative check: recognising a form of assessment
displayTitle: Which of these is a form of assessment, rather than another part of a module handbook?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is a form of assessment rather than another part of a module handbook?

_items.text: A presentation to the group, followed by a written report.
_items.feedback: Yes. A presentation and a report are both things you produce and are judged on.

_items.text: A reading list of three chapters each week.
_items.feedback: This is the reading, not an assessment.

_items.text: A timetable of weekly two-hour lectures.
_items.feedback: This is the schedule, not an assessment.

_items.text: A note that the module is worth twenty credits.
_items.feedback: This is an administrative detail, not an assessment.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A presentation and a report are work you produce and are marked on, so they are forms of assessment. The reading list, the timetable and the credit value are all parts of a handbook, but none of them is an assessment.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that describes something you produce and are judged on, not how the module is run.
_incorrect.final: The presentation and report are forms of assessment: work you produce and are marked on. The reading list, the timetable and the credit value are all parts of a module handbook, but none is an assessment in itself.

title: Formative check: formative or summative
displayTitle: Sort each of these assessments by whether it is formative or summative.
instruction: Choose Formative or Summative for each one, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Sort each assessment into formative or summative.

_items.text: A practice essay your tutor comments on but does not mark

_options.text: Formative
Summative

_items.text: A short quiz during term that does not count toward your grade

_options.text: Formative
Summative

_items.text: The end-of-module examination

_options.text: Formative
Summative

_items.text: The final coursework essay that sets your module grade

_options.text: Formative
Summative

_feedback.correct: That's right. Formative assessment is there to help you improve and does not count toward your grade; summative assessment is the task that sets it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. For each one, ask: does this count toward my final grade, or is it there to help me improve first?
_incorrect.final: The practice essay and the term quiz are formative: they help you improve and do not count. The examination and the final coursework essay are summative: they set your grade. The test is simple - does it count toward the mark, or help you reach it?

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some of those are right, but not all. Check each one against the question: does it count, or help you improve first?
_partlyCorrect.final: Formative tasks (the practice essay, the term quiz) help you improve and do not count; summative tasks (the examination, the final coursework essay) set your grade.

title: What is each comment asking for?
displayTitle: What is each comment asking for?
body: Feedback comments point to an action. Sort each comment by what it is asking you to do.
instruction: Choose the action each comment is asking for, then select Submit. You can try as many times as you like.
ariaQuestion: Sort each feedback comment by the action it is asking for.

_items.text: Your claims need more backing.

_options.text: Use citations to support your own argument
Plan a logical flow to your argument
Analyse and evaluate, do not just describe

_items.text: Where is your evidence for this?

_options.text: Use citations to support your own argument
Plan a logical flow to your argument
Analyse and evaluate, do not just describe

_items.text: This paragraph is hard to follow.

_options.text: Use citations to support your own argument
Plan a logical flow to your argument
Analyse and evaluate, do not just describe

_items.text: Your structure jumps around.

_options.text: Use citations to support your own argument
Plan a logical flow to your argument
Analyse and evaluate, do not just describe

_items.text: You describe the theory but do not evaluate it.

_options.text: Use citations to support your own argument
Plan a logical flow to your argument
Analyse and evaluate, do not just describe

_items.text: Push beyond summary to analysis.

_options.text: Use citations to support your own argument
Plan a logical flow to your argument
Analyse and evaluate, do not just describe

_feedback.correct: That's the idea. A feedback comment is rarely just a verdict; it points to an action. 'More backing' and 'where is your evidence' both ask you to use citations to support your argument; comments about following and structure ask you to plan a clearer, more logical flow; and 'describe but do not evaluate' asks you to analyse and evaluate, not just describe. Reading the action behind the words is how you act on feedback.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. For each comment, ask what it wants you to do next, not just what it says. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some of those are right. For the rest, ask what action the comment is pointing to, and try again.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students get the same comment on a draft: You describe the debate well, but you do not take a position.

{{learner-a}} reads the comment at face value, as a small complaint rather than an instruction, and misses the action it is asking for. Nothing changes in how {{learner-a}} works, so in the next assessment the same problem appears and the same comment comes back: the mistake has simply been repeated.

{{learner-b}} works out the action behind the comment: it is asking for a judgement, not more description. {{learner-b}} takes strategic steps to address it, planning the next piece around a clear position and weighing the evidence toward it. The next assessment takes a position, and the comment does not return.

Both read the same words. Only {{learner-b}} read the action behind them and acted on it. That is what feedback is for: it tells you what to do differently, and acting on it strategically is how your work improves.

title: Acting on feedback
body: Use these on any piece of feedback you receive, before you start your next piece of work.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Have I read all of the feedback, not just the mark?
For each comment, have I worked out the action it is asking me to take?
Have I noticed any comment that appears more than once across my work?
Have I written down one or two things to do differently next time?
If a comment is unclear, have I planned to ask the tutor what they meant?

title: Formative check: recognising a form of feedback
displayTitle: Which of these is a form of feedback?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is a form of feedback?

_items.text: Annotations your tutor has written in the margin of your essay.
_items.feedback: Yes. Margin annotations are feedback: comments on your work to help you improve.

_items.text: The submission deadline for the essay.
_items.feedback: This is a deadline, not feedback on your work.

_items.text: The word count stated in the brief.
_items.feedback: This is a requirement of the task, not feedback.

_items.text: The reading list for the module.
_items.feedback: This is the reading, not feedback.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Margin annotations are one of the many forms feedback takes - comments on your work meant to help you improve. A deadline, a word count and a reading list are all parts of a brief, but none of them is feedback.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that comments on your work to help you improve, not a rule of the task.
_incorrect.final: Feedback is comments on your work to help you improve - here, the margin annotations. The deadline, word count and reading list are all parts of the task brief, not feedback on what you produced.

title: Formative check: what is the comment asking
displayTitle: A tutor writes on your work: 'This is mostly description; I would like to see more of your own analysis.' What is this comment asking you to do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is this feedback comment asking you to do?

_items.text: Break the material down and show what it means and how convincing it is, rather than just reporting it.
_items.feedback: Yes. 'More analysis' asks you to examine and interpret, not just describe.

_items.text: Write more words overall.
_items.feedback: Length is not the issue; the comment asks for a different kind of thinking, not more of the same.

_items.text: Add more description to be thorough.
_items.feedback: The comment asks for less description and more analysis, not more description.

_items.text: Change the topic to something easier.
_items.feedback: The comment is about how you treat the material, not which material you choose.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A comment asking for more analysis is telling you to break the material down and show what it means and how convincing it is, rather than simply reporting it. It is not asking for more words or more description.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what kind of thinking the comment is asking for, not how much you write.
_incorrect.final: The comment asks you to analyse: to examine and interpret the material and show what it means, rather than just describe it. It is not about length, more description, or an easier topic.

title: Formative check: surface and deep learning
displayTitle: You are preparing for a seminar in {{context}}. Which approach shows deep learning rather than surface learning?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach shows deep learning rather than surface learning?

_items.text: Asking why the ideas matter and linking them to what you already know.
_items.feedback: Yes. Deep learning connects ideas and asks why, which is how {{context}} wants you to work with them.

_items.text: Reading the chapter once and highlighting the key terms to recall later.
_items.feedback: That is surface learning: the information is stored, but not connected or questioned.

_items.text: Making a clean copy of the lecture slides to revise from.
_items.feedback: Tidy notes help, but copying reproduces information rather than working with it.

_items.text: Memorising the definitions so you can repeat them accurately.
_items.feedback: Repeating definitions is surface learning; deep learning links them into understanding.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Deep learning links ideas and asks why they matter; the other options stop at taking in or reproducing information.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that connects ideas and asks why, rather than storing or reproducing them.
_incorrect.final: Deep learning means connecting ideas and asking why, not storing or reproducing them. In {{context}}, that is what taking part in the subject calls for.

title: Formative check: how teaching is organised
displayTitle: Thinking about how a module in {{context}} is put together, which statement best describes how its teaching is organised to build your learning?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How is a module's teaching organised to build your learning?

_items.text: Each session is designed to build towards the module's intended learning, not just to cover topics in turn.
_items.feedback: Yes. Teaching is designed around what you are meant to be able to do, so the parts connect.

_items.text: The sessions are a list of separate topics with no particular order.
_items.feedback: Modules are designed towards intended learning, so the order and links are deliberate, not random.

_items.text: Lectures exist to deliver facts; the rest of the module is optional.
_items.feedback: Every part, not only lectures, is designed to build the intended learning.

_items.text: The timetable is arranged mainly around room availability.
_items.feedback: Logistics aside, the teaching itself is organised around what the module wants you to learn.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A module's sessions are designed to build towards its intended learning, which is why the parts connect rather than stand alone.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about sessions building towards intended learning.
_incorrect.final: Teaching is organised around the module's intended learning: each part is designed to build towards what you should be able to do, so the sessions connect.

title: Formative check: the purpose of an assessment
displayTitle: A tutor in {{context}} sets a piece of coursework early in the module and returns detailed comments but no mark that counts. What purpose does this assessment mainly serve?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What purpose does this assessment mainly serve?

_items.text: To help you see how you are doing and improve before the work that counts.
_items.feedback: Yes. Assessment that informs and improves your learning is serving a formative purpose.

_items.text: To produce the final grade for the module.
_items.feedback: A piece with comments but no counting mark is not there to grade you.

_items.text: To rank you against other students on the course.
_items.feedback: Its purpose here is to guide your improvement, not to rank you.

_items.text: To check that you attended the session.
_items.feedback: Attendance aside, this assessment is set to help you learn, not to register presence.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An assessment like this serves a formative purpose: it shows you where you are and helps you improve before the work that counts.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about helping you improve before the work that counts.
_incorrect.final: This assessment serves a formative purpose: detailed comments with no counting mark are there to help you improve, not to grade or rank you.

title: Formative check: acting on feedback
displayTitle: You receive this comment on a piece of {{context}} work: ‘Your argument needs more support from evidence.’ Which response best turns it into a specific next action?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response best turns the comment into a specific next action?

_items.text: For my next draft, add specific evidence to each main claim and show how it supports the claim.
_items.feedback: Yes. That turns the comment into a concrete, checkable action you can take.

_items.text: Try harder to make my arguments better next time.
_items.feedback: That is a good intention, but it is too vague to act on; name what you will do, and to what.

_items.text: Feel disappointed that the work was not strong enough.
_items.feedback: A reaction is understandable, but it is not an action; decide what you will change.

_items.text: Wait to see whether the same comment comes up again.
_items.feedback: Waiting delays improvement; the comment already tells you what to act on now.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A specific next action names what you will do and to what, so you can carry it out and check it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that names a concrete, checkable step.
_incorrect.final: To act on feedback, turn the comment into a specific, checkable step, such as adding evidence to each claim and showing how it supports the claim, rather than a vague intention or a feeling.

title: Formative check: using the learning, assessment and feedback cycle
displayTitle: You want to use the learning, assessment and feedback cycle to study {{context}} better. Which plan best uses the whole cycle rather than one part of it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which plan best uses the whole cycle?

_items.text: Set myself a practice task, check it against the criteria, then use the feedback to change how I prepare next time.
_items.feedback: Yes. That moves through learning, assessment and feedback, and feeds back into your learning.

_items.text: Re-read my notes more times before the deadline.
_items.feedback: Repetition is one study habit, but it uses only the learning part, not assessment or feedback.

_items.text: Wait for my marks and read the comments at the end of the module.
_items.feedback: That uses feedback only, and too late to change how you learn during the module.

_items.text: Focus on getting the highest mark and ignore the comments.
_items.feedback: A mark alone, without acting on feedback, breaks the cycle you are trying to use.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Using the whole cycle means learning, checking your work against the criteria, then letting the feedback change how you study next.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that moves through learning, assessment and feedback.
_incorrect.final: A plan that uses the cycle moves through all three parts: you learn, you check your work against the criteria, and you let the feedback change how you study next time.
